clinicalPearls: Bleeding arising from the fragile germinal matrix, chiefly in preterm infants, with risk inversely related to gestation and birth weight
Most haemorrhages occur within the first few days of life
It is graded from small germinal matrix or intraventricular bleeding to large haemorrhage with ventricular dilatation or parenchymal involvement
Presentation ranges from clinically silent to a catastrophic decline with bulging fontanelle, seizures and shock
Cranial ultrasound is the mainstay of diagnosis and surveillance in at-risk infants
Post-haemorrhagic ventricular dilatation and parenchymal (grade IV) involvement carry the greatest risk of adverse outcome
reference.pathophysiology: In preterm infants the germinal matrix is a highly vascular, metabolically active region with fragile, poorly supported vessels. Immature cerebral autoregulation means fluctuations in cerebral blood flow and pressure, from hypotension, hypercapnia, ventilation or handling, are transmitted to these vessels and cause them to rupture. Blood may remain localised to the matrix or extend into the ventricles, and large haemorrhages can obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow causing ventricular dilatation, or be accompanied by venous infarction of adjacent white matter, which underlies the neurological sequelae.
additionalInvestigations: Cranial ultrasound for diagnosis, grading and serial monitoring
Measurement of head circumference and fontanelle assessment
Coagulation studies and full blood count
MRI where parenchymal injury or prognosis needs clarification
redFlags: Rapid neurological deterioration with a tense fontanelle
reference.prognosis: Low-grade haemorrhages often have a good outcome, whereas high-grade haemorrhage with parenchymal involvement or progressive ventricular dilatation carries a substantial risk of cerebral palsy and developmental impairment.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal neurological examination excludes haemorrhage
Failing to monitor for evolving ventricular dilatation
Overlooking modifiable haemodynamic factors that propagate bleeding
Not arranging neurodevelopmental follow-up after high-grade haemorrhage
